ES 348.description: Biological organisms and ecosystems with particular reference to mechanisms of change and human impacts on the environment. ES 355.description: A seminar that engages with people and communities impacted by climate change to document their experiences. Includes publishing, broadcasting and presenting the resulting stories with major media and cultural partners.

ES 361.title: The Biodiversity of British Columbia
ES 361.description: An overview of British Columbia's globally significant biodiversity. We examine species distribution patterns, use and conservation, including academic and government research and management. Lectures and field trips include synthesis of patterns of biodiversity, management success and failure and future biodiversity conservation and use in BC. Course goals include developing a deep understanding of the patterns of biodiversity in BC, explaining the reasons for these patterns and identifying numerous species and their importance.
ES 361.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:
  Complete all of the following:
    Complete all of: ES 200
    Complete 1 of: ES 240, BIOL 215

ES 365.title: Climate and Society
ES 365.description: A survey of the climate system and its interaction with past, present and future societies. Topics include: climate change and the onset of agriculture/domestication, climate change and the rise and fall of early civilizations, the anthropocene and global warming. The interplay between science, media, public relations and public policy is also addressed.

ES 370.title: Intermediate Field Study
ES 370.description: Further field-based study of environmental problems and solutions, such as integrating watershed scale analysis and enhancements. Typically offered in a compressed format. Additional fees may be necessary to support field expenses.

ES 371.title: Terroir Field School
ES 371.description: A mix of lectures and field trips in the Loire Valley, Brittany and Normandy. Examines how smaller terroir-driven food and wine producers create wealth in economic, ecological, social and cultural dimensions. Offered in English in collaboration with UVic partner university L'Ecole; Agricultures in Angers, France.

ES 378.title: Leadership Skills for Change
ES 378.description: Builds the skills necessary to lead effective change in community-engaged settings. Emphasis on personal and group communication skills, decision-making techniques, presentation and facilitation skills, ethics and self-awareness for leadership. Includes case studies, examinations of theories of leadership and social movements, and practical experience.
ES 378.prerequisite_text: Complete all of: ES200 - Introduction to Environmental Studies (1.5)

ES 380.title: Topics in Political Ecology
ES 380.description: An in-depth systematic examination of specific environmental areas through seminars and projects; the development of appropriate responses to questions and problems within the selected areas; modes of interaction and communication with professional and community groups; application of theory to practice; qualitative vs. quantitative research methods. This course is conducted as a seminar and may include a field trip for which a fee is charged. * Contact hours may vary depending on the topic.
ES 380.prerequisite_text: Complete all of: ES200 - Introduction to Environmental Studies (1.5)

ES 381.title: Topics in Ethnoecology
ES 381.description: An in-depth systematic examination of specific environmental areas through: seminars and projects; the development of appropriate responses to questions and problems within the selected areas; modes of interaction and communication with professional and community groups; application of theory to practice; qualitative vs. quantitative research methods. This course is conducted as a seminar and may include a field trip for which a fee is charged. * Contact hours may vary depending on the topic.
ES 381.prerequisite_text: Complete all of: ES200 - Introduction to Environmental Studies (1.5)

ES 382.title: Topics in Ecological Restoration
ES 382.description: An in-depth systematic examination of specific environmental areas through seminars and projects; the development of appropriate responses to questions and problems within the selected areas; modes of interaction and communication with professional and community groups; application of theory to practice; qualitative vs. quantitative research methods. Conducted as a seminar and may include a field trip for which a fee is charged. * Contact hours may vary depending on the topic.
ES 382.prerequisite_text: Complete all of: ES200 - Introduction to Environmental Studies (1.5)

ES 384.title: Natural and Social Systems Theory
ES 384.description: Reviews fundamental principles of systems theory and provides a foundation for further exploration and application of systems concepts. Examines concepts such as cybernetics, holism, boundaries, negative and positive feedback, self-organization and transformation. These principles are applied to both natural and social systems.
ES 384.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:
  Complete all of the following:
    Complete all of: ES 200
    Complete 1 of: ES 301, ES 321, ES 341

ES 399.title: Environmental Evidence in a Post-truth Era
ES 399.description: Builds the skills necessary to critically assess environmental issues and research. Emphasis is placed on critical assessment of evidence of all kinds, grounded in an understanding of quantitative and qualitative methodological considerations. Evaluates a wide variety of approaches to understanding and addressing real-world environmental challenges, and work towards producing their own compelling and comprehensive analysis of these challenges.
ES 399.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:
  Complete all of the following:
    Complete all of: ES 200, ES 240
    minimum third-year standing.
ES 399.prerequisite_text: Complete all of the following Complete all of: ES200 - Introduction to Environmental Studies (1.5) ES240 - Ecological Processes (1.5) minimum third-year standing.

ES 403.title: Field Course in Reconciliation, Ecology and Place-based Law
ES 403.description: Explores the structures of reconciliation, law, policy and sustainability in a specific territory on the west coast of BC. Analyzes co-existing Indigenous and state jurisdictional and governance systems that shape a region.

ES 404.title: Deep Roots, Trajectories of Environmental Thought
ES 404.description: Examines classic works and persistent themes in North American environmental thought. A study of primary source material and texts by writers such as Thoreau, Austin, Muir, Pinchot, Leopold, Carson, Ellul, Schumacher, Berry and Shiva.
ES 404.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:
  Complete all of: ES 200, ES 301
ES 404.prerequisite_text: Complete all of: ES200 - Introduction to Environmental Studies (1.5) ES301 - Political Ecology (1.5)

ES 405.title: Climate, Energy and Politics
ES 405.description: Focuses on developing the knowledge and skills necessary to evaluate how we might reshape energy systems to address the dual challenges of climate change and sustainability.
ES 405.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:
  Complete all of: ES 200, ES 301
ES 405.prerequisite_text: Complete all of: ES200 - Introduction to Environmental Studies (1.5) ES301 - Political Ecology (1.5)

ES 406.title: Alternative Economies for Social Change
ES 406.description: A consideration of the many forms of economic activity that go on outside competitive, profit-maximizing markets. The concept of 'social enterprise' is examined, with ways that communities, and not just individuals, develop their economies with goals of community benefit and social justice as well as material improvement. 'The economy' is treated as a landscape of different practices that may be obscured by concentrating just on market transactions.
ES 406.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:
  Complete all of: ES 200, ES 301
ES 406.prerequisite_text: Complete all of: ES200 - Introduction to Environmental Studies (1.5) ES301 - Political Ecology (1.5)

ES 407.title: Mindfulness, Sustainability and Social Change
ES 407.description: Examines how mindfulness training, particularly meditation, is being integrated into contemporary environmental and social change efforts. Current research on the physical, psychological, ecological and social benefits of mindfulness training are examined. Students are introduced to a variety of meditative practices as part of the course.

ES 408.title: Visual Ecology, Seeing the Wild
ES 408.description: Explores the terrain of visual media that inform environmental studies in B.C. and internationally. Environmental movements and media campaigns; the visuality of place; art and activism; Indigenous new media; representations and relations with non-human animals. Critically examines the politics of looking.
ES 408.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:
  Complete all of: ES 200, ES 301
ES 408.prerequisite_text: Complete all of: ES200 - Introduction to Environmental Studies (1.5) ES301 - Political Ecology (1.5)

ES 411.title: Environmental Solutions
ES 411.description: Partnering with the Environmental Law Centre, the course will draw on current ELC projects, students, clients and approaches. The cumulative work throughout the term is on a specific project for a community organization with direct support from the instructor.
ES 411.prerequisite_text: Complete all of: ES301 - Political Ecology (1.5)

ES 413.title: Indigenous political ecologies of the shoreline
ES 413.description: Focuses on coastlines, seabeds, river banks, flood plains and other spaces where water and earth meet, course material will draw from cross-disciplinary scholarship in Indigenous geography, law, politics, ecologies, and philosophies, as well as non-scholarly representations of Indigenous cultural practices, histories and resurgent struggles situated at the shore.

ES 417.title: Power, Difference, and Environmental Politics
ES 417.description: Explores how environmental politics is shaped by and seek to challenge relations of oppression.
ES 417.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:
  Complete all of: ES 200, ES 301
ES 417.prerequisite_text: Complete all of: ES200 - Introduction to Environmental Studies (1.5) ES301 - Political Ecology (1.5)

ES 421.title: Ethnobotany: Plants and Human Cultures
ES 421.description: An introduction to the study of the relationship between plants and human cultures, with a focus on the Indigenous peoples and environments of northwestern North America. Use of plants as foods, materials and medicines, plant nomenclature and folk classification, and the role of plants in religion and mythology are topics covered. There are one or more field trips.
ES 421.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:
  Complete all of: ES 200, ES 321
ES 421.prerequisite_text: Complete all of: ES200 - Introduction to Environmental Studies (1.5) ES321 - Ethnoecology (1.5)

ES 423.title: Traditional Systems of Land and Resource Management
ES 423.description: The role of traditional ecological knowledge in the understanding and documentation of the biodiversity of natural systems and their restoration. Examination of how restoration strategies can benefit from the close relationship of Indigenous Peoples to their local environments, and from their knowledge of plants and animals, their habitats and ecological interrelationships, as well as from traditional land and resource management strategies.
ES 423.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:
  Complete all of: ES 200, ES 321
ES 423.prerequisite_text: Complete all of: ES200 - Introduction to Environmental Studies (1.5) ES321 - Ethnoecology (1.5)

ES 425.title: Flowering Plant Diversity
ES 425.description: A regional and worldwide survey of flowering plants, including morphological diversity and adaptations; plant evolution and phylogeny; species concepts; modern classification and nomenclature; and experimental approaches to the study of plant diversity. Labs emphasize identification and use of keys. Lab projects include the option of a pressed plant collection. Contact instructor for details and collecting equipment.
ES 425.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:
  Complete all of the following:
    Complete all of: BIOL 184, BIOL 186
    and minimum third-year standing.
ES 425.prerequisite_text: Complete all of the following Complete all of: BIOL184 - Evolution and Biodiversity (1.5) BIOL186 - Physiology and Cell Biology (1.5) and minimum third-year standing.

ES 427.title: Colonization, Nature, and the Making of British Columbia
ES 427.description: Introduces students to the essential concepts and methods used by historians, archaeologists, anthropologists, geographers and others to analyze environmental change from prehistoric to modern times. Explores how cultural encounters between Euro-American and the Indigenous peoples of British Columbia played out on the physical landscape, focusing on the processes of dispossession and repossession that led to the creation of the space that became British Columbia.
ES 427.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:
  Complete all of: ES 200, ES 321
ES 427.prerequisite_text: Complete all of: ES200 - Introduction to Environmental Studies (1.5) ES321 - Ethnoecology (1.5)

ES 429.title: Urban Ethnoecology
ES 429.description: Cultural understandings of ecosystems and knowledge of interactions between human activities and human habitats in urban settings. Explores the ways city dwellers understand and interact with urban and peri-urban habitats. Surveys the intersections between people and place in cities from an ethnoecological perspective to inform and contribute to initiatives to create sustainable cities.
ES 429.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:
  Complete all of the following:
    Complete all of: ES 200
    minimum third-year standing.
ES 429.prerequisite_text: Complete all of the following Complete all of: ES200 - Introduction to Environmental Studies (1.5) minimum third-year standing.

ES 431.title: History, Science and Culture of Wine
ES 431.description: Documents the evolution of human civilization through the lens of wine, chronicles the transition from mysticism to industrial global commoditization. Workshops examine terroir, varietal, age, price, quality and value of viticulture and oenological traditions from around the world, and what "sustainability" means in this context.
ES 431.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:
  Complete all of the following:
    Complete all of: ES 200
    minimum third-year standing
    permission of the school.
ES 431.prerequisite_text: Complete all of the following Complete all of: ES200 - Introduction to Environmental Studies (1.5) minimum third-year standing permission of the school.

ES 433.title: Introduction to Permaculture Design
ES 433.description: The origins, theory and design methods of permaculture. Examines foundational texts that have influenced the development of permaculture, as well as contemporary permaculture texts. Critical examination of a range of designs and applications, including food systems, water systems, energy systems, appropriate technologies, place making, and the built environment.
ES 433.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:
  Complete all of the following:
    Complete all of: ES 200
    minimum third-year standing
  or permission of the school.
ES 433.prerequisite_text: Complete all of the following Complete all of: ES200 - Introduction to Environmental Studies (1.5) minimum third-year standing or permission of the school.

ES 434.title: Ethnoecology as Deep History
ES 434.description: Explores the deep history of sustainability, resilience and collapse in past societies. Examines how communities across cultures and throughout time managed ecosystems, food systems and urbanization, and how inequality and governance shaped resilience or vulnerability. Archaeological case studies highlight both fragility and innovation, offering lessons for today’s challenges in food security, biodiversity, governance and climate adaptation.

ES 443.title: Climate Change and Biodiversity
ES 443.description: Examines the challenges a changing climate poses for ecology and conservation biology research and management, including ecological restoration. Particular attention is given to reading scientific papers, both those that present biodiversity pattern and process changes, as well as those that present management solutions to climate-driven biodiversity loss.
ES 443.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:
  Complete all of: ES 200, ES 240, ES 341
ES 443.prerequisite_text: Complete all of: ES200 - Introduction to Environmental Studies (1.5) ES240 - Ecological Processes (1.5) ES341 - Past, Present, and Future Ecologies (1.5)

ES 445.title: Changing Nature
ES 445.description: Discusses responsible intervention in ecosystems undergoing rapid change, covering a wide range of contemporary issues from barcoding biodiversity to rewilding, all with the aim of pushing against boundaries of received knowledge about preservation, conservation and restoration of nature.
ES 445.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:
  Complete all of: ES 200, ES 341
ES 445.prerequisite_text: Complete all of: ES200 - Introduction to Environmental Studies (1.5) ES341 - Past, Present, and Future Ecologies (1.5)

ES 446.title: Sustainable Fisheries
ES 446.description: A practical examination of sustainable fisheries from a variety of interdisciplinary perspectives. Examines sustainability issues for fisheries and aquaculture through an integrated study of fish biology/ecology, oceanography, hydrology, environmental impact assessment, natural resource management and environment and land use planning.
ES 446.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:
  Complete all of the following:
    Complete all of: ES 200
    Complete 1 of: ES 321, ES 341
ES 446.prerequisite_text: Complete all of the following Complete all of: ES200 - Introduction to Environmental Studies (1.5) Complete 1 of: ES321 - Ethnoecology (1.5) ES341 - Past, Present, and Future Ecologies (1.5)

ES 449.title: Foundations of Restoration Ecology
ES 449.description: Examines ecological theories on topics including functional ecology, resilience and community assembly as classic ecological frameworks, as well as more complex socio-ecological contexts. Focuses on application of these concepts to environmental work, particularly ecological restoration. A reading course driven by student discussion and presentations aimed at graduate students and advanced undergraduates.
ES 449.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:
  Complete all of: ES 200, ES 341
ES 449.prerequisite_text: Complete all of: ES200 - Introduction to Environmental Studies (1.5) ES341 - Past, Present, and Future Ecologies (1.5)

ES 461.title: Environmental Impact Assessment
ES 461.description: An introduction to the objectives, philosophy, concepts, methods and social implications of environmental impact assessment (EIA). A critical examination of EIA as an analytical tool in the context of resource management and public policy is undertaken. Examples are drawn from BC, Canada and other countries.
ES 461.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:

    Complete all of: ES 200
    Complete 1 of: ES 301, ES 321, ES 341

ES 470.title: Advanced Field Study
ES 470.description: Study of environmental problems and solutions intended to be more self-directed where the student identifies a problem and designs the process to implement solutions. Typically offered in a compressed format. Additional fees may be necessary to support field expenses.

Prerequisites:

ES 471.title: Galiano Island Field Study
ES 471.description: Compressed format field study focused on regenerative and restorative designs for ecological and social resilience. Offered in partnership with the Galiano Conservancy Association with field portion based on Galiano Island. Additional fees are necessary to support field expenses.

ES 473.description: An advanced practical study of permaculture principles in an intensive field-based setting. Focus on implementing concepts and practicing skills introduced in ES 433.

EUS 200.title: Introduction to European Cultures and Identities
EUS 200.description: Explores the cultures and interconnectedness of national identities in Europe from Ancient Rome until the present. An interdisciplinary, team-taught approach provides students with a comprehensive understanding of European cultures through the study of art history, literature, film, music, folklore, geography and philosophical thought.

EUS 270.title: Culture, Economics and Politics of Europe
EUS 270.description: Examines the cultural, social, economic and political history of post-WWII Europe from an interdisciplinary perspective. Introduces key issues associated with the study of decolonization, European integration, migration and other important aspects that shaped the societies and cultures of modern Europe. Discusses the role of the European Union in Europe and the world.

EUS 311.title: Governments and Politics in Europe
EUS 311.description: Historical backgrounds to, institutional framework for, and players involved in, political conflict in European countries. Consideration is given to contemporary policy issues and the process of European integration.
EUS 311.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:
  Complete 1 of the following:
    Complete 1 of: EUS 100, EUS 270, ECON 270, POLI 211, SLLC 270
    or permission of the department
requirement_notes: Alternatively: or permission of the department

EUS 340.title: The Second World War and the Recovery of Western Europe
EUS 340.description: Examination of the effects of the Second World War on Europe, and the recovery of the Western European states in the postwar period.

EUS 400.title: The European Legacy
EUS 400.description: Explores the historical roots of current social, political and cultural issues in North America through an examination of Europe’s legacy in North America and our contemporary presuppositions of what it means to be Western and European. Provides a critical overview of the history of European ideas through the lens of contemporary topics such as human rights, decolonization, religious tolerance, diversity, euthanasia, etc.

EUS 470.title: Field School in European Studies
EUS 470.description: The academic element of the European Union Study Tour offered by the Network for European Studies Canada or another Study Tour/Field School with relevance to European Studies that is approved by the Program. Normally requires some course work to be completed prior to departure, while other course work is due during and after the field school. Content must be approved in advance by the Program.
EUS 470.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:
  Complete all of the following:
    Complete 1 of: EUS 270, ECON 270, SLLC 270, POLI 211
    Permission of the program.
EUS 470.prerequisite_text: Complete all of the following Complete 1 of: EUS270 - Culture, Economics and Politics of Europe (1.5) ECON270 - Culture, Economics and Politics of Europe (1.5) SLLC270 - Culture, Economics and Politics of Europe (1.5) POLI211 - European Integration and the European Union (1.5) Permission of the program.

EUS 470X.title: Compliance for Field School in European Studies
EUS 470X.description: The non-academic pre-departure preparation for the EU Study Tour, which is offered by the Network for European Studies (Canada) and administered through the University of Victoria. Successful enrolment in and completion of this course is a requirement for participation in the EU Study Tour.

EUS 490.title: Directed Reading in European Studies
EUS 490.description: Directed reading and/or a research project in European Studies under the supervision of a faculty member.

EUS 495.title: Directed Experiential Learning in European Studies
EUS 495.description: Individual examination of analytical issues in European Studies in relation to work, internship, volunteer activities, or other pre-approved activities under the guidance of a faculty member. Student and instructor must have agreed on learning objectives and methods of assessment before experiential learning opportunity begins. Learning opportunity must be distinct from any previous or concurrent Co-op work-term placements.

FA 100.title: Special Topics in Fine Arts
FA 100.description: A multi-disciplinary investigation into various aspects of the arts. Focus may vary from year to year.

FA 101.title: Creative Being
FA 101.description: An exploration of the diversity within creative practice and theory that builds bridges across disciplines and challenges students' understanding of the creative process.

FA 200.title: Special Topics in Fine Arts
FA 200.description: A multi-disciplinary investigation into various aspects of the arts. Focus may vary from year to year.

FA 201.title: Introduction to Professional Practice
FA 201.description: Introduction to workplace professional practice expectations in preparation for Fine Arts co-op work terms. Includes preparation of cover letters and résumés, skills assessment and analysis, networking, interview skill development and career planning.

FA 245.title: The Arts and Technology I
FA 245.description: An introductory course focusing on ideas central to the interrelationship between various arts and technologies.

FA 300.title: Interdisciplinary Studies
FA 300.description: Emphasizes an interdisciplinary approach to contemporary artistic concerns. In each year, coursework focuses on a particular issue.

FA 301.title: Fine Arts Field School
FA 301.description: Intensive, in-situ experiential learning in one or more of the fine arts disciplines. Topic may vary from year to year. Includes travel in or outside Canada.

FA 305.title: Theory and Practice of Film and Video Direction
FA 305.description: Introduction to basic narrative patterns in film and video with an emphasis on image systems, plot and character, sound, and scene construction. Development and translation of a script into pictures using digital cameras and video editing software.

FA 335.title: Popular Culture
FA 335.description: An interdisciplinary examination of the popular arts and their place in society. The topics for examination vary in different years and sections.

FA 346.title: The Arts and Technology II
FA 346.description: A practice-oriented seminar, focusing on the use of computer technology in the arts. Areas for consideration may vary from year to year.

FA 360.title: Theoretical and Critical Issues in the Arts
FA 360.description: A special topics course that examines critical and theoretical issues as they relate to the visual, literary and performing arts. Areas for consideration vary from year to year.

FA 399.title: Directed Studies in Fine Arts
FA 399.description: Individual research in Fine Arts taken under the supervision of a faculty member. Permission of faculty member supervising the project and approval of the Associate Dean.

FRAN 100.title: Level A1 Intensive French
FRAN 100.description: Development of beginner language skills and intercultural competencies, through oral and written practice, to build the building blocks for communication and interaction, focusing on basic vocabulary, pronunciation, and simple grammar structures (familiar everyday expressions, personal details). Exploration of differences and cultural diversities in French-speaking regions and countries. Advances to an A1 level of the European Common Framework for Languages. Prepares for upper-beginner (A2) study upon completion.

FRAN 120.title: Level A2 Intensive French
FRAN 120.description: Sequel to FRAN 100. Development of upper-beginner language skills and intercultural competencies to facilitate communication and interaction in simple, routine situations (description of background and needs; frequently used expressions), through oral and written practice. Exploration of differences and cultural diversities in French-speaking regions and countries. Advances to an A2 level of the European Common Framework for Languages. Prepares for intermediate (B1) study upon completion.

FRAN 125.title: Showcasing the Francophonie (in English)
FRAN 125.description: An introduction to French-speaking cultures through diverse research into cultural and linguistic topics around the global French-speaking world.

FRAN 150.title: French Conversation
FRAN 150.description: Develops listening comprehension and oral expression, and introduces students to varied oral discourses to help them function in diverse Francophone contexts.

FRAN 265.description: Explore the diversity of the Francophonie from Quebec to Senegal, France to Vietnam. Instruction and media are presented in French, but students have the option to hand in assignments in English.

FRAN 275.description: Practice of writing and reading in a variety of forms. In-depth study of grammatical features to improve writing skills.

FRAN 280.description: Analysis of a selection of major texts and media in French from different traditions, times and genres, illustrating the changing notion of literariness.

FRAN 305.description: A continuation of FRAN200 dealing with the subject matter of linguistics as it relates to the French language. Covers sentence structures, meaning, and sociolinguistics.

FRAN 310.title: Literature, Media and Culture II
FRAN 310.description: A close reading and analysis of literary texts and media in French. Analytical and critical approaches to texts and media vary.

FRAN 325.title: Studies in the Cultures of the French-speaking World (in English)
FRAN 325.description: Study of cultures in the French-speaking world using a variety of sources.

FRAN 325A.title: The Tour de France (in English)
FRAN 325A.description: Offered online and concurrently with the Tour in July. Explores the sport, history, politics and business of one of the world’s toughest sporting events: representations of the Tour in culture (literature, film, media); globalization of the Tour as a mega sporting and cultural event; and ethical debates surrounding doping and commercialization in sport, as well as the lack of equal gender representation.

FRAN 327.title: Voodoo in Popular Francophone Culture and Fiction (in English)
FRAN 327.description: Introduces the basic concepts of the religion of voodoo in Africa, the Francophone Caribbean and Louisiana. Differentiates facts from fiction, especially in terms of recognizing the stereotypes emanating from Hollywood and understanding the authentic bases and elements of a religion practiced by over 25 million people in the world. Includes an experiential learning component.

FRAN 335.title: Cinema of the French-Speaking World (in English)
FRAN 335.description: Cinema and the relationship of cinema with literature and culture in the French-speaking world.

FRAN 336.title: Québec and Francophone Cinema (in English)
FRAN 336.description: Examines the main events and cultural trends that have defined Quebec society and the Francophonie, as reflected in film. The course is taught in English, and all films include English subtitles.

FRAN 345.title: Advanced French Language
FRAN 345.description: Focuses on usages of French as represented in the Francophonie. Reflects on oral and written discourses in several contexts. Students produce written and oral documents in French. Brings students to a C1.1 level of the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages.

FRAN 360.description: An advanced, field-based exploration of the literatures, cultures and expressive forms in the French-speaking world. Areas of investigation may, depending on the year, be selected in Europe, North America, Africa or the Caribbean. An additional field trip fee may be applied.

FRAN 360A.title: Paris on Stage
FRAN 360A.description: A field-based exploration of Paris, seen as a theatrical stage and a living museum. Explores how Paris stages itself in the past and in the present, and how French civilization through the arts (in particular theatre, and the visual arts) tells tales of the world and ways of being part of the world. One week of coursework on campus followed by two weeks of study and travel in Paris. Offered in French; an additional field trip fee applies.

FRAN 378.title: Creative Writing in French
FRAN 378.description: A practical introduction to creative writing. Covers fundamentals such as narration, intrigue, dialogue, point of view, characters, description, creative process, as well as public reading. Active participation in various exercises, lectures and plenary discussions to explore the many characteristics of creative writing and refine use of language to go beyond the commonplace, clichés and stereotypes and produce original, creative work in multiple genres. Exercises include work in short story, poetry, theatre and non-fiction writing.

FRAN 384.description: Deals with word formation and word markers (stems, morphemes, prefixes, suffixes, etc.) and sentence structures in French.

FRAN 394.title: Children's and Young Adult Literature in French
FRAN 394.description: Children’s and young adult’s literature in French from a perspective that immediately grants literary value to the phenomenon. A survey of the Francophone production, from fairy tale to fantasy, from comic books to poetry. Explores the vast and varied literary production destined for children and young adults, and will analyze it for academic and teaching purposes. Includes an experiential learning component.

FRAN 401.title: Teaching and Learning French
FRAN 401.description: Explores the field of teaching and learning French from a myriad of perspectives, with a focus on strategies and other language teaching issues. Theoretical in pedagogical approach, but practical in learning outcomes. Exposes students to a corpus of short readings and other online materials pertinent to teaching and learning French; they then apply the theoretical knowledge gained from those reading materials by designing language community-group projects, participating in classroom discussions and online forums, and presenting individual projects in class or in the community.

  or permission of the school.

FRAN 404.title: History of French
FRAN 404.description: The evolution of the French language from the eighth to the 18th century. Through the study of representative literary and non-literary texts in the original, in relation to historical circumstances, students acquire familiarity with major social and cultural events and become aware of the diversity and the mobility of the language.

FRAN 405.title: Varieties of French
FRAN 405.description: A survey of historical and (socio)linguistic aspects of French as spoken in different areas. Focus can be on French in North America, Africa, the Caribbean, Europe or another area, highlighting the vitality and richness of this language by pointing out specificities of varieties of French.

FRAN 407.title: Canadian Francophonie and Linguistic Ideologies
FRAN 407.description: Explores the main linguistic ideologies about French in Canada (especially in minority settings), their shaping and influence on language policies and their manifestations among French speakers, including attitudes, beliefs and linguistic insecurity. Debunks language stereotypes.

FRAN 409.description: Advanced development of listening and speaking skills in French to help students gain more fluency and spontaneity of speech while also developing more accuracy, inventiveness and critical expression. Listening to recordings from various media (radio broadcasts, newsflashes, documentaries, interviews, etc); speaking exercises such as reading, commenting, or debating. FRAN 412.title: History of Québec and Franco-Canadian Literature
FRAN 412.description: A survey of Québec and Franco-Canadian literature from New France to the turn of the 21st century. Introduction to Québec and Franco-Canadian culture. Fiction, poetry, drama, non-fiction and cinema. Study of selected works in their historical, political, sociological and cultural context.

FRAN 418.title: Québec Literature and Culture of the Extrême Contemporain
FRAN 418.description: Examines the literary and artistic movements of the contemporary era in Québec through reading and analyzing works published or released since 2000. Explores major theoretical concepts such as postmodernism. Includes fiction, non-fiction, poetry, drama and other literary genres, as well as cinema, music and other artistic forms.

FRAN 422.title: Contemporary Francophone African Novel
FRAN 422.description: The Francophone African novel in the second half of the 20th century and the first part of the 21st century. Screening of African films to highlight issues in the novels selected.

FRAN 426.title: Indigenous Literatures of Canada or the Francophone World
FRAN 426.description: Focuses on works of First Nations, Métis and Inuit writers published in French in Canada and studies them in their historical, political, sociological and cultural context. May also cover Indigenous literature written in French in other geographical areas, such as the Maghreb and the Pacific Ocean, connecting them with issues of resistance and resurgence as they appear in Canada.
FRAN 426.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:
  Complete all of: FRAN 310
  or permission of the school.
FRAN 426.prerequisite_text: Complete all of: FRAN310 - Literature, Media and Culture II (1.5) or permission of the school.

FRAN 428.title: Francophone African Women Filmmakers
FRAN 428.description: Over the last two decades African women documentary filmmakers have been at the forefront of the renewal of image making on the African continent. Examines the conditions under which they have emerged and gained prominence. Examines how, following their male counterparts, they have imagined the world, articulated their gender identities and, in the process, created new, different styles of documentary film-making.
FRAN 428.requirement_summary:
Pre- or corequisites:
  Completed or concurrently enrolled in all of: FRAN 310
  or permission of the school.
FRAN 428.prerequisite_text: Completed or concurrently enrolled in all of: FRAN310 - Literature, Media and Culture II (1.5) or permission of the school.

FRAN 430.title: Studies in French Literatures and Culture before 1800
FRAN 430.description: The studies of texts and traditions linked by genre, period, movement or theme, within their historical and cultural contexts.
FRAN 430.requirement_summary:

FRAN 431.title: Medieval Literature
FRAN 431.description: Study of a number of medieval literary works in translation, with occasional readings of the original texts. Students will acquire some familiarity with medieval French culture and languages, as well as a sense of literature in its many histories. Media, art, gender theory, religious studies and modern literary theory will be used to give contexts and life to the readings.
FRAN 431.requirement_summary:

FRAN 434.title: Medieval and Renaissance Theatre
FRAN 434.description: Medieval and Renaissance plays in the original. Through a selection of dramatic texts, students explore the conditions of theatrical representations before theatres were built in stone. Places farces, miracles, sotties and comedies in the context of religious holidays, Carnival, or school plays.
FRAN 434.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:

FRAN 436.title: Early Modern Literature and Culture
FRAN 436.description: Study of a number of Early Modern works in the original. Students acquire some familiarity with Early Modern French culture and languages, as well as a sense of the emergence of new ideas about the world and about the humanity of humankind. Media, art, gender theory, historiography and modern literary theory give contexts and life to the readings.
FRAN 436.requirement_summary:

  Earn a minimum grade of B in each of the following: FRAN 275
  or permission of the school.

  or permission of the school.

FRAN 437.title: French Myths up to the 21st Century
FRAN 437.description: Understanding myths as collective narratives and enduring representations that inform a world view and a sense of community, this course examines some of the French literary creations and figures that became cultural icons, such as the Grail, the melancholy poet, the "Noble Savage," the "City of the Ladies," Asterix, or the famous "French touch." Looking at the fabric of memory, culture and literature, the course surveys the making of symbols and shared references and emphasizes the role of intercultural exchanges in the production of these myths.

FRAN 438.title: French Texts that Made our World
FRAN 438.description: Measures the lasting impact of seminal French literary works, from Abelard’s autobiography to Simone de Beauvoir's Le Deuxième Sexe or the "French theory" that toppled accepted authorities and traditions well beyond their original times and places. By providing historical and intellectual contexts, as well as close readings and conceptual tools, it retraces the threads of transmission and influence of foundational, although revolutionary, ideas and texts.

FRAN 445.title: Nature and the Environment in French-Speaking Cultures
FRAN 445.description: Explores the representations, thoughts and the position of human beings within their natural environment in the arts (literature, theatre, film, paintings) from the 16th century to the present. Through key concepts such as the anthropocene and the nature-culture dualism, and by using theoretical approaches such as eco/geocriticism and ecofeminism, exposes students to new ways of understanding how we can critically and sensitively re-imagine the environmental humanities today and into the future.
FRAN 445.requirement_summary:
Pre- or corequisites:
  Completed or concurrently enrolled in all of: FRAN 310
  or permission of the school.
FRAN 445.prerequisite_text: Completed or concurrently enrolled in all of: FRAN310 - Literature, Media and Culture II (1.5) or permission of the school.

FRAN 449.title: Critical and Subversive French Theatre
FRAN 449.description: Examines how Theatre, as an art, but also as a political and media phenomenon, has questioned the representations of news since the 17th century, and how this reveals a subversive and critical culture on stage.
FRAN 449.requirement_summary:
Pre- or corequisites:
  Completed or concurrently enrolled in all of: FRAN 310
  or permission of the school.
FRAN 449.prerequisite_text: Completed or concurrently enrolled in all of: FRAN310 - Literature, Media and Culture II (1.5) or permission of the school.

FRAN 450.title: Studies in French Literature and Culture after 1800
FRAN 450.description: A selection of major texts linked by genre, period, movement, or theme, studied within their historical and cultural context.
FRAN 450.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:

FRAN 451.title: Women in the World of French Theatre
FRAN 451.description: Women’s dramatic writing, actresses’ memoirs, audience reactions and character studies from a cultural and historical perspective.
FRAN 451.requirement_summary:
Pre- or corequisites:
  Completed or concurrently enrolled in all of: FRAN 310
  or permission of the school.
FRAN 451.prerequisite_text: Completed or concurrently enrolled in all of: FRAN310 - Literature, Media and Culture II (1.5) or permission of the school.

FRAN 455.title: Dada, Surrealism and the End of the French Novel
FRAN 455.description: The rise of the greatest artistic movement of the 1920s and 1930s in France and Europe out of the ashes of WWI.
FRAN 455.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:
  Ability to understand oral and written French.
requirement_notes: Ability to understand oral and written French.

FRAN 456.title: 20th-Century French Theatre
FRAN 456.description: The distinctive characteristics of modern theatre and of major theatrical movements; plays illustrating different themes and theatrical styles.
FRAN 456.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:

FRAN 458.title: French Thought from Descartes to Postmodernism and Beyond
FRAN 458.description: Examines conceptions of the individual and the subject from Enlightenment Humanism to contemporary Posthumanisms. Looks at philosophy, literature and culture more generally in order to understand how identity is conceived.

FRAN 459.title: The Everyday in French Culture since the 19th Century
FRAN 459.description: The importance of the everyday life of citizens became central after the French Revolution, as seen in various artistic, intellectual and mediatic expressions. Looks at the many representations of the everyday all the way to contemporary culture, society and politics in the French-speaking world.
FRAN 459.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:
  Complete all of: FRAN 310
  or permission of the school.
FRAN 459.prerequisite_text: Complete all of: FRAN310 - Literature, Media and Culture II (1.5) or permission of the school.

FRAN 470.title: Studies in Cultures of the French-Speaking World
FRAN 470.description: Offerings devoted to the culture, literature or language of the French-speaking world. May include genre, thematic or cross-cultural topics.
FRAN 470.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:

  or permission of the school.
Pre- or corequisites:

  or permission of the school.

FRAN 471.title: Figures on the Fringe
FRAN 471.description: Exploration and analysis of heroes or villains from various cultural origins of the French-speaking world.

FRAN 478.title: Critical Methods
FRAN 478.description: Develops and deepens critical reading based on methodological tools and theoretical notions specific to culture (literature, cinema, or theatre) and the media.
FRAN 478.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:
  Complete all of: FRAN 310, FRAN 375
  or permission of the school.
FRAN 478.prerequisite_text: Complete all of: FRAN310 - Literature, Media and Culture II (1.5) FRAN375 - Writing in French II (1.5) or permission of the school.

FRAN 499.title: Honours Graduating Essay
FRAN 499.description: During the final year of the Honours program, students write a graduating essay in French of approximately 7,500 to 10,000 words under the direction of a member of the school; the topic is approved by the Honours Committee. The essay must conform to acceptable standards of style and format and be submitted before the end of second term classes. An oral examination in French covering the topic of the essay is conducted by a committee of three persons (normally, the faculty supervisor, the second reader, and the school Honours Adviser).

Prerequisites:

GDS 201.title: Global Development
GDS 201.description: An introduction to global development and contemporary issues facing the Global South (Africa, Latin America and Asia). Focuses on theoretical, historical and policy debates shaping global development. Topics may include: colonization anddecolonization; post-colonial nation-state building; democratization; global poverty and inequality; food security; culture and development; international development assistance and the role of international organisations, NGOs and social movements in shaping development.

GDS 300.title: Contemporary Challenges in Global Development
GDS 300.description: A critical review of contemporary challenges in global development, including a selection of topics related to key areas of focus for official development assistance such as foreign aid, poverty alleviation and development; gender, human rights and democracy; environmental sustainability and public health; transnationalism, migration and mobility; conflict and displacement; food security, water and energy resources; Indigenous issues; and struggles and development challenges in the Global South.
GDS 300.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:
  Complete 1 of: GDS 201, GEOG 211, POLI 217
GDS 300.prerequisite_text: Complete 1 of: GDS201 - Global Development (1.5) GEOG211 - Political and Economic Geography (1.5) POLI217 - Global Development (1.5)

GDS 301.title: Working in Global Development
GDS 301.description: Essential skills required for effective practical engagement with issues in global development including topics such as advocacy, cross-cultural communication, project management and evaluation, community based research, fundraising, community organizing and management of non-profits.

GDS 390.title: Special Topics in Global Development Studies
GDS 390.description: Presents selected topics in an emerging field related to global development or one not covered in-depth in regular offerings.
GDS 390.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:
  Complete 1 of: GDS 201, POLI 217
  or permission of the program.
GDS 390.prerequisite_text: Complete 1 of: GDS201 - Global Development (1.5) POLI217 - Global Development (1.5) or permission of the program.

GDS 391.title: Politics of Environment and Development Field School
GDS 391.description: An advanced, field-based exploration of the politics of environment and global development, focusing on the challenges of inclusive and sustainable development. Topics may include: farming and food security; urbanization and pollution; mining and extractive growth strategies; local experiences of climate change; anti-poverty initiatives and community resilience; legal rights and political movements in ethnic minority communities; and local support for refugee and undocumented communities. A field trip fee may be applied.
GDS 391.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:
  Complete all of: POLI 103
  Complete 1 of: GDS 201, POLI 217
  or permission from the department(s).
GDS 391.prerequisite_text: Complete all of: POLI103 - The Worlds of Politics (1.5) Complete 1 of: GDS201 - Global Development (1.5) POLI217 - Global Development (1.5) or permission from the department(s).

GDS 400.title: Recasting and Rethinking Global Development
GDS 400.description: An advanced interdisciplinary seminar on contemporary issues and debates in global development. Engages with theoretical and real-world policy challenges while rethinking conventional approaches to development grounded in western assumptions of progress. Topics may include gender, human rights, decolonization, environmental sustainability, migration, political economy of resource extraction, labour, ethical trade, south-south trade, food security and eco-tourism. Assignments include applied learning, interdisciplinary projects and research.
GDS 400.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:
  Complete 1 of: GDS 201, POLI 217
  minimum third-year standing
  or permission of the program
GDS 400.prerequisite_text: Complete 1 of: GDS201 - Global Development (1.5) POLI217 - Global Development (1.5) minimum third-year standing or permission of the program

GDS 490.title: Directed Studies in Global Development
GDS 490.description: Individual study of a specific research topic in global development studies under the supervision of a faculty member.

GDS 491.title: Directed Experiential Learning in Global Development
GDS 491.description: Individual examination of issues in global development studies in relation to work or volunteer activities directly related to global development. Issues to be explored and methods of assessment to be confirmed with instructor before the experiential learning opportunity begins. Must include at least 150 hours of work or volunteer activities. Assessment normally involves a reflective journal and final paper.

GEOG 100.title: Geography for Today
GEOG 100.description: Each topic stretches the geographical imagination by offering a new lens through which to view the relationship between people and the richly diverse and varied environments they inhabit. From the intimate personal places of one individual's human experience to the worldwide reach of global-scale physical environmental changes that impact everyone, the complex challenges and opportunities of today's world are illuminated with the help of an integrated spatial perspective. Topic may change from year to year.

GEOG 101A.title: Environment, Society and Sustainability
GEOG 101A.description: Introduction to the functioning of the biosphere, the ways in which humans alter natural processes, environmental consequences of these alterations and the implications for sustainability. Topics include: energy flows, biogeochemical cycles, ecosystem structure and dynamics, pollution, global change, water resources, biodiversity, endangered species, protected areas, agriculture and food, forestry, marine resources, poverty and development and different worldviews. Potential for a sustainable society is discussed.

GEOG 101B.title: Space, Place and Society
GEOG 101B.description: Introduction to foundational spatial concepts, theories and approaches in human geography including geographies of identity and place; urban landscapes and planning; population and migration; and global geopolitics. Up-to-the-minute real-world examples at multiple scales are used to demonstrate the importance of where something happens in the world.

GEOG 103.title: Our Natural Earth
GEOG 103.description: Introduces the science of Physical Geography using an earth-systems approach. Course themes include global climates and climate change, hydrology and water resources, geomorphology and natural hazards, and biogeography; with focus on how geographic sciences are applied to address real world issues.

GEOG 104.title: Our Digital Earth
GEOG 104.description: Introduces students to how geospatial technologies influence our daily lives and shape the world around us. Students learn how to collect and utilize location-based data, develop web maps and mobile mapping apps, create technologies to respond to environmental disasters and humanitarian crises, and think spatially in order to improve our understanding of our planet.

GEOG 130.title: Climate Change
GEOG 130.description: An introduction to the fundamental physical principles governing the climate of the Earth system, and its response to anthropogenic factors. Topics include components of the climate system, radiative energy balance, forcings and feedbacks, the carbon cycle, climate of the past, impacts of climate change, global climate model projections, and approaches to mitigation and adaptation.

GEOG 209.title: Environmental Management
GEOG 209.description: Critically interrogates approaches to the management or governance of environments and natural resources. Themes may include parks and protected areas, fisheries, forestry, water and energy management; environmental impact assessment; comprehensive land-use and marine spatial planning; and urban sustainability, all in the context of profound political and environmental change, colonialism, and Indigenous resurgence.

    Complete all of the following:

      declared Honours or Major in Climate Science.
requirement_notes: declared Honours or Major in Climate Science.

GEOG 211.title: Political and Economic Geography
GEOG 211.description: Examines the major thematic concerns that have traditionally shaped the sub-disciplines of political and economic geography, while also engaging with emerging issues that are likely to become focal points in shaping future debates. Explores the co-constitutive relationship between politics, economics and space.
GEOG 211.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:
  Complete all of the following:
    Complete all of: GEOG 101B
    minimum second-year standing.
GEOG 211.prerequisite_text: Complete all of the following Complete all of: GEOG101B - Space, Place and Society (1.5) minimum second-year standing.

GEOG 218.title: Social and Cultural Geography
GEOG 218.description: Introduction to current themes and issues in social and cultural geography with a focus on the interpretation of cultural landscapes, place-making and the spatial expression of dynamic social identities. Lab assignments involve original field observations, honing quality academic writing skills and innovative approaches to reflecting on the relation between popular culture, society and landscape.
GEOG 218.prerequisite_text: Complete all of: GEOG101B - Space, Place and Society (1.5)

GEOG 220.title: Weather and Climate
GEOG 220.description: An introduction to the physical processes that determine Earth’s weather and climate. Topics include atmospheric composition, flows of energy through the atmosphere, small-scale and large-scale winds, cloud and precipitation processes, climate change.
GEOG 220.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:
  Complete all of the following:
    Complete 1.5 units of: 100 level PHYS
    Complete 1.5 units of: 100 level MATH
    or permission of the department.
GEOG 220.prerequisite_text: Complete all of the following Complete 1.5 units of: 100 level PHYS Complete 1.5 units of: 100 level MATH or permission of the department.

GEOG 222.title: Introduction to GIS
GEOG 222.description: Introduces techniques and fundamentals of spatial data and analysis. Topics include: scale, map interpretation and Geographic Information Systems.

GEOG 226.title: Quantitative Methods in Geography
GEOG 226.description: Application of statistical techniques to the analysis of geographic problems. Topics include measurement, hypothesis formulation, sampling strategies, parametric and nonparametric statistical tests.
GEOG 226.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:
  Complete 1 of the following:
    Complete 3 units from GEOG 100 - 299
    Complete 3 units from EOS 100 - 299
GEOG 226.prerequisite_text: Complete 1 of the following Complete 3 units from GEOG 100 - 299 Complete 3 units from EOS 100 - 299

GEOG 227.title: Qualitative Research Methods in Geography
GEOG 227.description: Introduces a range of qualitative research approaches and tools applied in Geography. The course describes and examines a range of guiding paradigms (ethnography, participatory action research, the scientific method, indigenous methodologies, Marxism and Feminism) and data collection tools (from survey and questionnaires, focus groups, interviews, or participant observation to arts-based methods including photo voice and participatory video). Hands-on learning includes designing a research project, collecting data, analyzing the results (coding, data interpretation, thematic and interpretive analysis) and presenting the findings.

GEOG 228.title: Introduction to Remote Sensing
GEOG 228.description: Introduces the use of remotely sensed images to address information issues related to both physical and human geography. Students are exposed to a range of image types and resolutions, as well as methods and tools used for their analysis.

GEOG 230.title: Introduction to Environmental Data Analysis
GEOG 230.description: An introduction to using computer programming to analyze climate data. Topics include fundamentals of programming, data visualization, analysis of spatial data, descriptive statistics, linear regression.
GEOG 230.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:
  Complete all of the following:
    Complete 1.5 units of: 100 level MATH
    Complete 1 of: EOS 110, EOS 130, GEOG 103, GEOG 130
    or permission of the department.
GEOG 230.prerequisite_text: Complete all of the following Complete 1.5 units of: 100 level MATH Complete 1 of: EOS110 - Oceans and Atmosphere (1.5) EOS130 - Climate Change (1.5) GEOG103 - Our Natural Earth (1.5) GEOG130 - Climate Change (1.5) or permission of the department.

GEOG 252.title: Coastal Geography
GEOG 252.description: Explores a wide variety of coastal topics from biophysical, ecological, and social-economic perspectives. Topics focus on coastal landscapes and communities that may include fundamentals of coastal oceanography, climate, biodiversity, water quality, fisheries, indigenous people, tourism and implications for management.

GEOG 272.title: Climatology and Hydrology
GEOG 272.description: An investigation of the fundmental processes controlling climate and hydrology. Explores various factors and interactions that determine the spatial and temporal variations of individual climate elements. Focuses on the mutual interaction of climate with the Earth's surface and the role that ground surface type or cover plays in moderating local climate and hydrology.
GEOG 272.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:
  Complete 1 of: GEOG 103, GEOG 110, GEOG 130, EOS 110, EOS 130
GEOG 272.prerequisite_text: Complete 1 of: GEOG103 - Our Natural Earth (1.5) GEOG110 - Oceans and Atmosphere (1.5) GEOG130 - Climate Change (1.5) EOS110 - Oceans and Atmosphere (1.5) EOS130 - Climate Change (1.5)

GEOG 274.title: Biogeography
GEOG 274.description: Examines the relationships among organisms - principally plants and animals - and their environment, emphasizing their distributions across a range of spatial and temporal scales. Examines basic ecological and evolutionary concepts affecting biogeographic processes of dispersal, speciation and extinction; how patterns of biodiversity change over space and time from early earth history to the contemporary environment; the nature of changing biotic distributions with increasing human impacts and global change.
GEOG 274.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:
  Complete all of: GEOG 101A, GEOG 103
GEOG 274.prerequisite_text: Complete all of: GEOG101A - Environment, Society and Sustainability (1.5) GEOG103 - Our Natural Earth (1.5)

GEOG 276.title: Geomorphology
GEOG 276.description: Introduction to Earth surface process and landforms including riverine, desert, coastal, glacial, hillslope and permafrost environments. Focus on regional and Canadian landscapes. Involves a field trip.
GEOG 276.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:
  Complete 1 of: GEOG 103, GEOG 120, EOS 120
GEOG 276.prerequisite_text: Complete 1 of: GEOG103 - Our Natural Earth (1.5) GEOG120 - The Dynamic Earth (1.5) EOS120 - The Dynamic Earth (1.5)

GEOG 301.title: Environmental Impact Assessment
GEOG 301.description: An introduction to the objectives, philosophy, concepts, methods and social implications of environmental impact assessment (EIA). A critical examination of EIA as an analytical tool in the context of resource management and public policy is undertaken. Examples are drawn from B.C., Canada and other countries.
GEOG 301.prerequisite_text: Complete all of: GEOG209 - Environmental Management (1.5)

GEOG 303.title: Conservation and Ecology of Whales
GEOG 303.description: Examines the fundamental biology, evolution and ecology of the modern whale species. Discusses the history and the spectrum of the human relationships with whales. Current topics in the marine mammal sphere are critically examined.
GEOG 303.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:
  Complete 1 of: GEOG 274, BIOL 150A, BIOL 184, BIOL 190B
GEOG 303.prerequisite_text: Complete 1 of: GEOG274 - Biogeography (1.5) BIOL150A - Modern Biology (1.5) BIOL184 - Evolution and Biodiversity (1.5) BIOL190B - General Biology II (1.5)

GEOG 306.title: Geography of Canada
GEOG 306.description: Explores the physical, historical, cultural, and political geography of Canada. Topics may include: human / environment relationships; settlement and development patterns; colonialism and Indigenous resurgence; national identity and conflict; and current issues in the Canadian context.

GEOG 309.title: Geography of British Columbia
GEOG 309.description: An examination of the physical, economic, and cultural landscapes that distinguish the cities and rural regions of Canada's West Coast province.

GEOG 310.title: Global Migration
GEOG 310.description: Contemporary issues relating to the patterns, processes, and politics of global migration. Theories, concepts and themes associated with cross-border migratory flows are explored as they relate to the increase in global migration and mobility of people of different nationalities and cultural backgrounds around the world. Topics include border control and security, demographic patterns of movement relating to refugees and internally-displaced persons, human smuggling and trafficking.

GEOG 313.title: Field Studies in Mountain Meteorology
GEOG 313.description: An immersive opportunity to understand the physical processes of meteorological phenomena in mountain environments. Measuring and monitoring of snowpack, extreme weather and climate and their associated hazards in mountain ranges are prominent course themes. A field trip fee may be applied.
GEOG 313.prerequisite_text: Complete all of: GEOG272 - Climatology and Hydrology (1.5)

GEOG 314.title: Global Environmental Change and Human Response
GEOG 314.description: Based on four components: global environmental change; sustainable development; biodiversity; and population impoverishment and environmental degradation. Lectures and discussion emphasize the causes of global change, the present and expected impacts on natural and social systems, and response strategies that have been proposed or enacted.

GEOG 315.title: Geocaching
GEOG 315.description: Introduces the activity of geocaching, the fundamentals of GPS navigation and data collection. Emphasis is placed on geocaching, the history and workings of GPS and associated navigation systems, map datums and coordinate systems and basics of GPS data management. Hands-on operating and working with GPS units in the field, through a variety of geocaching activities and assignments. Examples of the use of GPS in geographical research is demonstrated through lectures and readings.

GEOG 316.title: Field Studies in Human Geography
GEOG 316.description: Explores concepts and concerns of human geography including personal, cultural and political considerations of space, place and society through practical, experiential learning. A field trip fee may be applied.
GEOG 316.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:
  Complete all of the following:
    Complete all of: GEOG 101A, GEOG 101B
    Complete 1 of: GEOG 209, GEOG 211, GEOG 218
  or permission of the department.

GEOG 317.title: Field Studies in Sustainable Communities
GEOG 317.description: The challenges and opportunities for promoting resilient, inclusive, equitable and sustainable communities are explored through practical and experiential learning. A field trip fee may be applied.
GEOG 317.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:
  Complete all of the following:
    Complete all of: GEOG 101A, GEOG 101B
    Complete 1 of: GEOG 209, GEOG 211, GEOG 218
  or permission of the department.

GEOG 318.title: Indigenous Geographies
GEOG 318.description: An examination of the development of Indigenous approaches, praxis, and thought in the field of geography historically and contemporaneously, through a critical engagement with the works of Indigenous scholars in the field of geography and related disciplines, alongside a critical analysis of broader developments in geography and its implications for Indigenous peoples.

    Complete 1 of: GEOG 209, GEOG 211, GEOG 218
    Or permission of the instructor.

GEOG 319.title: Remote Sensing of the Environment using Passive Sensors
GEOG 319.description: Focuses on physical principles underlying passive remote sensing and electromagnetic propagation in free space and matter; attenuation, absorption and scattering mechanisms; interaction of energy with the atmosphere and Earth materials such as vegetation, soil, rock, water and urban structures.

GEOG 322.title: Remote Sensing of the Environment using Active Sensors
GEOG 322.description: Processing and analysis of remote sensing data collected using active sensors – those that transmit their own energy. Data from active microwave sensors, including RADAR and Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) sensors, are discussed and analyzed with respect to their applicability as standalone and complementary data sources to remote sensing data acquired using passive systems. Laboratory assignments use image analysis software in a variety of applications.

GEOG 323.title: Digital Mapping
GEOG 323.description: Introduces thematic mapping. Emphasis on cartographic data manipulation, generalization and symbolization; map design, visualization and communication.

GEOG 324.title: Directions in Geography
GEOG 324.description: Explores changing perspectives, approaches, and traditions in geography, focusing on the discipline’s rich history as well as its potential future directions. Introduces students to current leaders in the field of geography and considers how students can contribute to shaping the future of the discipline through their own personal life directions.
GEOG 324.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:
  4.5 units of 100- or 200-level GEOG courses.

GEOG 328.title: GIS Analysis
GEOG 328.description: Focuses on analysis for digital mapping and modeling, developing and using geographic data to answer spatial research questions, conducting basic spatial interpolations and carrying-out multi-criteria modelling.

GEOG 329.title: GIS Applications and Tools
GEOG 329.description: The basics of GIS tool development including applications, desktop GIS customization, model building in a GIS environment, online GIS, and building web pages that include GIS maps and tasks.

GEOG 332.title: Urban Development in the Global South
GEOG 332.description: Examines fundamental characteristics of cities in the Global South with a focus on urban organization, questioning development from a social, cultural, economic and environmental perspective in the region. Addresses the driving forces as well as resulting challenges of urban growth and investigates the consequences of these transformations in terms of human development and environmental sustainability. Discusses and analyses contentious urban issues following a problem-based and solution-oriented approach applied to case studies from the Global South.

GEOG 333.title: Contemporary Challenges in Global Development
GEOG 333.description: A critical review of contemporary challenges in global development, including a selection of topics related to key areas of focus for official development assistance such as foreign aid, poverty alleviation and development; gender, human rights and democracy; environmental sustainability and public health; transnationalism, migration and mobility; conflict and displacement; food security, water and energy resources; Indigenous issues; and struggles and development challenges in the Global South.
GEOG 333.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:
  Complete 1 of: GEOG 211, GDS 201, POLI 217
GEOG 333.prerequisite_text: Complete 1 of: GEOG211 - Political and Economic Geography (1.5) GDS201 - Global Development (1.5) POLI217 - Global Development (1.5)

GEOG 339.title: Disaster Management and Community Resilience
GEOG 339.description: Explores hazard events and the factors and conditions that lead to disasters. Covers such events as earthquakes, hurricanes, tsunamis, floods, droughts and examines their human and natural dimensions.Emphasis on understanding vulnerability and risk assessment, sustainable hazards mitigation and disaster management approaches to enhancing community resilience.
GEOG 339.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:
  Complete all of: GEOG 103, GEOG 211, GEOG 218
GEOG 339.prerequisite_text: Complete all of: GEOG103 - Our Natural Earth (1.5) GEOG211 - Political and Economic Geography (1.5) GEOG218 - Social and Cultural Geography (1.5)

GEOG 340.title: Cities and Planning
GEOG 340.description: Overview of key thematic areas related to cities and planning in the North American context. Includes a critical examination of the history of urban planning and contemporary issues in urban geography to foster a deeper appreciation of the spatial politics of the urban experience.
GEOG 340.prerequisite_text: Complete 1 of: GEOG211 - Political and Economic Geography (1.5) GEOG218 - Social and Cultural Geography (1.5)

GEOG 346.title: Health, Environment and Community
GEOG 346.description: Examines the dynamics and linkages between health and the environment at the micro scale of individuals to the macro scale of communities and nations. Definitions of health, wellness and well-being, as well as healthy communities; focusing on the range of factors, conditions and determinants that make people and place healthy or unhealthy.
GEOG 346.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:
  Complete 1 of: GEOG 209, GEOG 211, GEOG 218
GEOG 346.prerequisite_text: Complete 1 of: GEOG209 - Environmental Management (1.5) GEOG211 - Political and Economic Geography (1.5) GEOG218 - Social and Cultural Geography (1.5)

GEOG 353.title: Coastal and Marine Resource Management
GEOG 353.description: An integration of the scientific, cultural, and policy dimensions of resource management in coastal and marine systems. Concepts will be illustrated with examples from wildlife and fisheries management. Although global context is set, a special focus will be on British Columbia’s coast.
GEOG 353.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:
  Complete 1 of the following:
    Complete 1 of: GEOG 209, GEOG 252
    permission of the instructor.
GEOG 353.prerequisite_text: Complete 1 of the following Complete 1 of: GEOG209 - Environmental Management (1.5) GEOG252 - Coastal Geography (1.5) permission of the instructor.

GEOG 358.title: Landscape Ecology
GEOG 358.description: Landscape ecology emphasizes the interaction between spatial pattern and ecological processes. Focus is on the role of spatial heterogeneity in affecting the distribution and abundance of organisms, mass and energy transfers, and alterations of this structure by natural or anthropogenic forces. Implications for wildlife management and conservation are discussed.
GEOG 358.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:

    Complete 1 of: GEOG 101A, GEOG 103
    Complete 1 of the following:
      Complete all of: GEOG 226
      1.5 units minimum 200 level STAT or equivalent

GEOG 370.title: Methods in Hydrology
GEOG 370.description: An overview of hydrological processes, measurement techniques and data analysis. The movement of water in the hydrologic cycle via precipitation, interception, evapotranspiration, surface runoff, infiltration, soil moisture, groundwater flow and streamflow generation are examined. Applied aspects and local examples are discussed. Involves laboratory assignments and a field trip.
GEOG 370.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:
  Complete all of the following:
    Complete 1 of the following:
      Complete all of: GEOG 272
      Completed or concurrently enrolled in all of: EOS 340
    1.5 units 100 level Math
    minimum third-year standing.
review_reasons: alternatives GEOG 272, EOS 340 mix completed-only and concurrent options; stored as completed-only

GEOG 371.title: Water Resources Management
GEOG 371.description: A study of water resources management in different parts of the world, examining the influence of various physical, economic, social, political and technological factors. Examines the alternative ways in which such problems as water scarcity, floods and declining water quality are handled. Examines in detail a number of major water development schemes. Students are expected to undertake a modest research project and report upon it.
GEOG 371.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:
  Complete all of: GEOG 209, GEOG 272
GEOG 371.prerequisite_text: Complete all of: GEOG209 - Environmental Management (1.5) GEOG272 - Climatology and Hydrology (1.5)

GEOG 373.title: Applied Climatology
GEOG 373.description: A study of the application of physical principles to practical problems in climatology and the reciprocal interaction between climate and human activities. Topics include: urban effects on climate; air pollution; human bioclimatology; agricultural climatology; and methods of microclimatic modification.
GEOG 373.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:
  Complete all of the following:
    Complete all of: GEOG 272
    1.5 units 100 level MATH
    minimum third-year standing.
GEOG 373.prerequisite_text: Complete all of the following Complete all of: GEOG272 - Climatology and Hydrology (1.5) 1.5 units 100 level MATH minimum third-year standing.

GEOG 376.title: Process Geomorphology
GEOG 376.description: An investigation of the physical processes that create and maintain landforms. Focus on measurement and analysis of morphodynamic processes in fluvial, aeolian, coastal, glacial, hillslope, and/or periglacial landscapes (e.g., sediment transport, erosion, wind/wave energy, river discharge, glacial dynamics, weathering rates).
GEOG 376.requirement_summary:

    Complete 1 of the following:
      Complete all of: GEOG 276
      Complete all of: EOS 120, EOS 201
    Complete 1.5 units from MATH 100 - 199
    minimum third-level standing.

GEOG 380.title: Community Mapping
GEOG 380.description: Examines the theory and practice of community based mapping and how it can facilitate dialogue and collaborative partnering, thus leading to knowledge co-creation, planning, citizen empowerment and engagement, building consensus, more informed policy making and ultimately social justice. This course is designed to be action-oriented and experiential, and has a very high local field component.

GEOG 386.title: Contemporary Geopolitics
GEOG 386.description: An overview of global geopolitics and the transformation of the world political map. Examination of key concepts and approaches to contemporary geopolitics through a series of regional case studies.

GEOG 388.title: Topics in Regional Studies
GEOG 388.description: Geography of a selected region of the world from a systematic perspective. Topics may include: the physical and human landscape; settlement; economic, political and social geography; spatial variation in modernization and economic growth.

GEOG 391.title: Topics in Geography
GEOG 391.description: Examination of a specific topic or area in Geography. Topic(s) are provided in advance of registration. * Contact hours may vary depending on the topic.

GEOG 392.title: Topics in Applied Geography
GEOG 392.description: Examines applied dimensions of geography through experiential learning, emphasizing practical approaches and techniques used to analyze and address diverse topics.

GEOG 405.title: Dynamics of the Cryosphere
GEOG 405.description: Explores the dynamics of the four main elements of the Earth's cryosphere - glaciers, snow cover, floating ice and permafrost - in physical, climatological, hydrological and Earth system contexts. A field trip fee may be applied.
GEOG 405.requirement_summary:

GEOG 406.title: Sustainable Cities
GEOG 406.description: Explores the opportunities and challenges of creating ecologically-minded, resilient, healthy, and socially just cities with a practical, community-engaged focus.
GEOG 406.requirement_summary:
Prerequisites:
  Complete 2 of: GEOG 209, GEOG 332, GEOG 340, GEOG 346

GEOG 409.title: Personal Space
GEOG 409.description: Collective exploration of how geographical interests in gender, sexuality and identity intersect with a student's own personal and unique spaces of reflection, action and interaction. Themes may include: Feminist, Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Trans, Non-binary, Queer, Two-Spirit and Masculinist discourses as they relate to geographies of social justice; the reciprocal role of space in the creation, loss, and (re)claiming of identities; the body as a site of struggle; and intersectionality with a wide variety of lived experiences.

GEOG 411.title: Co-creating Research for Sustainable Futures
GEOG 411.description: Theory and practice of Community-based Participatory Research (CBPR) with a special focus on addressing community-identified research needs linked to the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (UN SDG). Familiarizes students with the UN SDGs and explores CBPR as an important mechanism for bridging diverse and co-created knowledges into local action through community partnerships.
